items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “whether a reason or piece of evidence actually bears on the conclusion”?
items.answer: Relevance
items.markingKey: Relevance: whether a reason or piece of evidence actually bears on the conclusion. [1]

items.stem: In Pelora, turnout at the general election was 67% in 2018 and 58% in 2023. Which conclusion can be reliably drawn?
options: Turnout will fall again at the next election
Voters were less interested in politics in 2023
Turnout fell by 9 percentage points between 2018 and 2023
Fewer people voted in 2023 than in 2018
items.answer: Turnout fell by 9 percentage points between 2018 and 2023
items.markingKey: Only the change in percentage points follows; the number of voters depends on the size of the electorate, and interest or future trends are not shown. (67 − 58 = 9 points.) [1]

items.stem: In Halvoria, turnout at the general election was 65% in 2014 and 57% in 2019. Which conclusion can be reliably drawn?
options: Turnout fell by 8 percentage points between 2014 and 2019
Voters were less interested in politics in 2019
Turnout will fall again at the next election
items.answer: Turnout fell by 8 percentage points between 2014 and 2019
items.markingKey: Only the change in percentage points follows; the number of voters depends on the size of the electorate, and interest or future trends are not shown. (65 − 57 = 8 points.) [1]

items.stem: Read the argument: “Corruption thrives when deals are hidden from public view. The EU Digital Services Act (2022) requires very large platforms to assess and reduce risks to elections. A survey of 30 people in Bogotá found most agreed. Therefore, every government should publish all public contracts online.” Explain why the survey evidence is insufficient to support the conclusion.
items.answer: Only 30 people in one city were asked; they may not be representative, and agreement does not show that the policy would work.
items.markingKey: 1 mark small/local sample; 1 mark opinion ≠ effectiveness [2]

items.stem: Read the argument: “Targeted governments can blame foreigners for economic hardship. Australia has had compulsory voting since 1924 and Belgium since 1893. A survey of 40 people in Lima found most agreed. Therefore, economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour.” (a) Explain why the survey evidence is insufficient to support the conclusion. (b) Identify an assumption needed for the conclusion to follow.
items.answer: (a) Only 40 people in one city were asked; they may not be representative, and agreement does not show that the policy would work. (b) The purpose of sanctions is to change the target’s behaviour rather than to signal disapproval.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark small/local sample; 1 mark opinion ≠ effectiveness [2] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the reasons given for the view that governments should ban live facial recognition in public places are sufficient to justify it? Consider different perspectives in your answer.
items.answer: For: It records everyone, not only suspects. Mistaken identifications fall more often on some ethnic groups. A 2019 study by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology found higher false-match rates for some demographic groups in many algorithms. Against: It relies on the assumption that the harm to innocent people outweighs the benefits for public safety. It does not fully answer the objection that the technology helps police find missing people and dangerous suspects. Judgement: A supported judgement tests relevance, sufficiency and assumptions, and says what extra evidence would be needed.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “whether the reasons and evidence given are enough to justify the conclusion”?
items.answer: Sufficiency
items.markingKey: Sufficiency: whether the reasons and evidence given are enough to justify the conclusion. [1]

items.stem: In Marvona, turnout at the general election was 76% in 2015 and 72% in 2019. Which conclusion can be reliably drawn?
options: Turnout will fall again at the next election
Fewer people voted in 2019 than in 2015
Turnout fell by 4 percentage points between 2015 and 2019
items.answer: Turnout fell by 4 percentage points between 2015 and 2019
items.markingKey: Only the change in percentage points follows; the number of voters depends on the size of the electorate, and interest or future trends are not shown. (76 − 72 = 4 points.) [1]

items.stem: Read the argument: “Much exported plastic is not recycled but burned or dumped. The EU AI Act (2024) restricts real-time remote biometric identification by police in public spaces to narrow exceptions. A survey of 40 people in Doha found most agreed. Therefore, richer countries should be banned from exporting plastic waste.” (a) Explain why the survey evidence is insufficient to support the conclusion. (b) Identify an assumption needed for the conclusion to follow.
items.answer: (a) Only 40 people in one city were asked; they may not be representative, and agreement does not show that the policy would work. (b) Exporting countries could manage the waste better at home.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark small/local sample; 1 mark opinion ≠ effectiveness [2] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: Which flaw in reasoning involves drawing a general conclusion from too few or untypical cases?
items.answer: Hasty generalisation
items.markingKey: Hasty generalisation: drawing a general conclusion from too few or untypical cases. [1]

items.stem: Which flaw is shown in this argument? “In 2019, Jovania decided to lower the voting age to 16 for local elections first. Two years later, trust in government rose. Clearly the policy caused this.”
items.answer: Post hoc (false cause)
items.markingKey: Post hoc (false cause): assuming that because one event followed another, the first caused the second. [1]

items.stem: Which flaw is shown in this argument? “We should ignore Leila’s argument that upstream countries should agree dam operations with downstream neighbours: Leila has never held a proper job.”
items.answer: Ad hominem
items.markingKey: Ad hominem: attacking the person making an argument rather than the argument itself. [1]

items.stem: Read these two extracts from a debate about the export of plastic waste to poorer countries. Extract 1: “If we agree to make producers pay for collection and recycling (extended producer responsibility) now, it will be only the first step: ever more extreme measures will follow, and before long ordinary people will have no freedom left.” Extract 2: “Elena asked 12 people at a café in Jakarta and 9 of them said the exporting governments should ban exports and build domestic recycling capacity. This proves that most people in the country support it.” (a) Name the flaw in Extract 1. (b) Name the flaw in Extract 2.
items.answer: (a) Slippery slope. (b) Hasty generalisation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: Read these two extracts from a debate about threats to press freedom. Extract 1: “In 2017, Kestria decided to fund public-interest journalism through independent trusts. Two years later, trust in government rose. Clearly the policy caused this.” Extract 2: “If we agree to raise press freedom in trade and aid agreements now, it will be only the first step: ever more extreme measures will follow, and before long ordinary people will have no freedom left.” (a) Name the flaw in Extract 1. (b) Explain why the reasoning in Extract 2 is flawed.
items.answer: (a) Post hoc (false cause). (b) It relies on claiming that one step will inevitably lead to a chain of extreme consequences without evidence.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark identifies feature; 1 mark explains why conclusion does not follow [2]

items.stem: Read these two extracts from a debate about state use of facial recognition surveillance. Extract 1: “In 2021, Lunaria decided to allow it only with a court warrant and independent audits. Two years later, trust in government rose. Clearly the policy caused this.” Extract 2: “Jonas asked 10 people at a café in Accra and 8 of them said the exporting governments should restrict exports of surveillance technology to countries with poor human rights records. This proves that most people in the country support it.” (a) Name the flaw in Extract 1. (b) Name the flaw in Extract 2. (c) Suggest how one of the extracts could be rewritten to avoid the flaw.
items.answer: (a) Post hoc (false cause). (b) Hasty generalisation. (c) e.g. Extract 1: replace the flawed move with relevant evidence, such as “a 2019 study by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology found higher false-match rates for some demographic groups in many algorithms”, and a reason linked to the conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark [1] (c) 1 mark identifies change; 1 mark improved reasoning [2]

items.stem: Read this argument about state use of facial recognition surveillance: “It records everyone, not only suspects. People who say that governments should ban live facial recognition in public places really want to tear down every existing institution overnight. That is absurd, so their view should be rejected. Governments should ban live facial recognition in public places, because this is clearly what should happen, and what should happen is that governments should ban live facial recognition in public places. Therefore, governments should ban live facial recognition in public places.” (a) Identify two flaws in the argument. (b) Identify the strongest part of the argument and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Straw man; Circular reasoning. (b) “It records everyone, not only suspects” — it is a relevant reason that does not rely on a flaw.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark identification; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: Read this argument about reform of the UN Security Council: “A single country can block action supported by most of the world. If we agree to abolish or restrict the veto for cases of mass atrocities now, it will be only the first step: ever more extreme measures will follow, and before long the whole political system will collapse. Samuel asked 12 people at a university debate in Hanoi and 10 of them said the UN member states should add new permanent members such as the G4 (Brazil, Germany, India, Japan) and African states. This proves that most people in the country support it. Therefore, the veto power of the permanent members should be restricted.” (a) Identify the strongest part of the argument and explain why. (b) Evaluate how far the argument supports its conclusion.
items.answer: (a) “A single country can block action supported by most of the world” — it is a relevant reason that does not rely on a flaw. (b) Only weakly: once the flawed parts are removed, one reason remains, without evidence; the conclusion may still be true but this argument does not establish it.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark identification; 1 mark explanation [2] (b) 1 mark judgement; 1 mark remaining support; 1 mark distinguishes weak argument from false conclusion [3]

items.stem: Which flaw in reasoning involves drawing a general conclusion from too few or untypical cases?
items.answer: Hasty generalisation
items.markingKey: Hasty generalisation: drawing a general conclusion from too few or untypical cases. [1]

items.stem: A speaker says: “Sofia asked 8 people at a café in Kuala Lumpur and 5 of them said the national government should create planned relocation schemes within countries. This proves that most people in the country support it.” Identify the flaw.
items.answer: Hasty generalisation
items.markingKey: Hasty generalisation: drawing a general conclusion from too few or untypical cases. [1]

items.stem: “A famous footballer said in an interview that voting should be made compulsory, so it must be true.” Name the flaw in this reasoning and explain why it weakens the argument.
items.answer: Appeal to inappropriate authority: the argument relies on relying on the opinion of someone who has no expertise on the subject, so the conclusion does not follow from the reasons given.
items.markingKey: 1 mark names flaw; 1 mark explains how it applies here; 1 mark effect on conclusion [3]

items.stem: Read these two extracts from a debate about the use of economic sanctions. Extract 1: “People who say that economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour really want to abolish all national borders immediately. That is absurd, so their view should be rejected.” Extract 2: “The government of Zentara has criticised Halvoria over the use of economic sanctions. But Zentara has the same problem itself, so the criticism is worthless.” Suggest how one of the extracts could be rewritten to avoid the flaw.
items.answer: e.g. Extract 1: replace the flawed move with relevant evidence, such as “decades of US sanctions on Cuba since the 1960s have not changed its system of government”, and a reason linked to the conclusion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies change; 1 mark improved reasoning [2]

items.stem: Explain whether you agree that flaws in reasoning are more common in political debate about disputes over shared rivers than in academic writing about it. Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.answer: For: Politicians and campaigners aim to persuade quickly, using ad hominem, slippery slope or appeals to popularity. Social media rewards emotional, simplified arguments. Against: Academic writing is peer reviewed, which removes many flaws. Academics can still generalise from small samples or confuse correlation with causation. Judgement: Flaws appear in both, but the purpose and checks of each type of writing affect how common they are.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (2 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (3–4 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [4]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “how well its reasons and evidence support its conclusion”?
items.answer: Strength of an argument
items.markingKey: Strength of an argument: how well its reasons and evidence support its conclusion. [1]

items.stem: Argument A: “They are forced to leave their homes through no fault of their own. This is supported by official statistics from the national statistics office covering the whole country. Some argue that widening the definition could weaken protection for people fleeing persecution, but a separate protocol could protect climate migrants without changing the 1951 Convention. So people displaced by climate change should be given legal refugee status.” Argument B: “We should ignore Ravi’s argument that people displaced by climate change should be given legal refugee status: Ravi dresses badly on television. Widening the definition could weaken protection for people fleeing persecution. This is supported by an interview with one family in Lagos. So it is wrong to say that people displaced by climate change should be given legal refugee status.” Which argument is stronger?
items.answer: Argument A
items.markingKey: Argument A uses better-quality evidence, considers the other side and avoids flaws. [1]

items.stem: Argument A: “If we agree to negotiate a basin-wide water-sharing treaty now, it will be only the first step: ever more extreme measures will follow, and before long we will have lost control of our own country. Downstream countries depend on the river for drinking water and farming. This is supported by an online poll on a campaign website. So upstream countries should agree dam operations with downstream neighbours.” Argument B: “Upstream countries have the right to use resources on their own territory. This is supported by a report by an independent international organisation. Supporters point out that downstream countries depend on the river for drinking water and farming, but this does not outweigh the costs. So it is wrong to say that upstream countries should agree dam operations with downstream neighbours.” Which argument is stronger?
items.answer: Argument B
items.markingKey: Argument B uses better-quality evidence, considers the other side and avoids flaws. [1]

items.stem: Argument A: “We should ignore Jonas’s argument that governments should ban live facial recognition in public places: Jonas has never held a proper job. It records everyone, not only suspects. This is supported by a press release from a company that would profit from the outcome. So governments should ban live facial recognition in public places.” Argument B: “The technology helps police find missing people and dangerous suspects. This is supported by a peer-reviewed study comparing 18 countries over ten years. Supporters point out that it records everyone, not only suspects, but this does not outweigh the costs. So it is wrong to say that governments should ban live facial recognition in public places.” Identify a flaw in Argument A.
items.answer: Argument A begins with a flawed claim (e.g. appeal to popularity, slippery slope, straw man or ad hominem) that gives no real reason.
items.markingKey: 1 mark flaw named; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Argument A: “We should ignore Sipho’s argument that the veto power of the permanent members should be restricted: Sipho has never held a proper job. A single country can block action supported by most of the world. This is supported by a press release from a company that would profit from the outcome. So the veto power of the permanent members should be restricted.” Argument B: “The veto keeps the great powers inside the UN system. This is supported by official statistics from the national statistics office covering the whole country. Supporters point out that a single country can block action supported by most of the world, but this does not outweigh the costs. So it is wrong to say that the veto power of the permanent members should be restricted.” (a) Compare the evidence used in the two arguments. (b) Identify a flaw in Argument A.
items.answer: (a) A uses a press release from a company that would profit from the outcome; B uses official statistics from the national statistics office covering the whole country. Argument B’s evidence is larger-scale, more independent or more systematic. (b) Argument A begins with a flawed claim (e.g. appeal to popularity, slippery slope, straw man or ad hominem) that gives no real reason.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark identifies each; 1 mark comparison of quality [2] (b) 1 mark flaw named; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Argument A: “It records everyone, not only suspects. This is supported by official statistics from the national statistics office covering the whole country. Some argue that the technology helps police find missing people and dangerous suspects, but these aims can be met with targeted searches authorised by a judge. So governments should ban live facial recognition in public places.” Argument B: “People who say that governments should ban live facial recognition in public places really want to tear down every existing institution overnight. That is absurd, so their view should be rejected. The technology helps police find missing people and dangerous suspects. This is supported by an interview with one family in Istanbul. So it is wrong to say that governments should ban live facial recognition in public places.” Compare and evaluate the two arguments. Which is more convincing? In your answer consider reasoning, evidence, use of language and the perspectives each represents.
items.answer: Argument A is more convincing: its evidence (official statistics from the national statistics office covering the whole country) is more reliable and representative, it responds to the opposing view, and it avoids flawed appeals. The other relies on an interview with one family in Istanbul and a flawed opening claim. However, both rest on assumptions, e.g. that the harm to innocent people outweighs the benefits for public safety, and more evidence would be needed for a firm judgement.

However, both rest on assumptions, e.g. that without the veto the Council would act more effectively on crises, and more evidence would be needed for a firm judgement.

items.stem: Argument A: “A democracy works best when governments are chosen by the whole electorate. This is supported by a report by an independent international organisation. Some argue that compulsory voting removes the freedom not to vote, but voters may still spoil their ballot or choose “none of the above”. So voting should be made compulsory.” Argument B: “People who say that voting should be made compulsory really want to abolish all national borders immediately. That is absurd, so their view should be rejected. Compulsory voting removes the freedom not to vote. This is supported by a press release from a company that would profit from the outcome. So it is wrong to say that voting should be made compulsory.” Compare and evaluate the two arguments. Which is more convincing? In your answer consider reasoning, evidence, use of language and the perspectives each represents.
items.answer: Argument A is more convincing: its evidence (a report by an independent international organisation) is more reliable and representative, it responds to the opposing view, and it avoids flawed appeals. The other relies on a press release from a company that would profit from the outcome and a flawed opening claim. However, both rest on assumptions, e.g. that governments chosen by more of the electorate will be more representative of the electorate’s interests, and more evidence would be needed for a firm judgement.

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the absence of contradictions between the claims in an argument”?
items.answer: Consistency

items.stem: “Turnout in Istrana rose after online voting was introduced. Therefore online voting increased turnout in Istrana.” Explain whether the reason given is sufficient to support the conclusion.
items.answer: Not sufficient: the reason is relevant, but the conclusion also needs it to be true that nothing else that could explain the rise changed at the same time; more evidence is needed to rule out other explanations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark judgement (insufficient); 1 mark identifies the gap/what else is needed; 1 mark explains why [3]

items.stem: “Fendaria has signed the Paris Agreement. Therefore Fendaria will cut its emissions.” Explain whether the reason given is sufficient to support the conclusion.
items.answer: Not sufficient: the reason is relevant, but the conclusion also needs it to be true that signing an agreement means a country will carry out its commitments; more evidence is needed to rule out other explanations.

items.answer: For: Downstream countries depend on the river for drinking water and farming. Agreed rules reduce the risk of conflict. The Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan (1960) has survived several wars. Against: It relies on the assumption that countries will keep to an agreement once it is signed. It does not fully answer the objection that upstream countries have the right to use resources on their own territory. Judgement: A supported judgement tests relevance, sufficiency and assumptions, and says what extra evidence would be needed.

items.stem: “The reasons given for the view that governments should repeal broad “false news” laws are sufficient to justify it.” To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Such laws are vague and let officials decide what is true. A free press is needed to expose corruption. Press freedom organisations have documented journalists jailed under “false news” laws in several countries. Against: It relies on the assumption that governments cannot be trusted to judge fairly what counts as false news. It does not fully answer the objection that false reports can cause panic during a crisis. Judgement: A supported judgement tests relevance, sufficiency and assumptions, and says what extra evidence would be needed.

items.stem: “Either the education ministry must run citizenship education programmes in schools, or we accept that low voter turnout among young people will never be solved. There is no other choice.” Name the flaw in this reasoning and explain why it weakens the argument.

items.stem: Read these two extracts from a debate about state use of facial recognition surveillance. Extract 1: “Millions of people have shared posts saying that governments should ban live facial recognition in public places, so it must be the right policy.” Extract 2: “In 2019, Valdoria decided to allow it only with a court warrant and independent audits. Two years later, the number of protests fell. Clearly the policy caused this.” Suggest how one of the extracts could be rewritten to avoid the flaw.
items.answer: e.g. Extract 1: replace the flawed move with relevant evidence, such as “a 2019 study by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology found higher false-match rates for some demographic groups in many algorithms”, and a reason linked to the conclusion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies change; 1 mark improved reasoning [2]

items.stem: Read these two extracts from a debate about threats to press freedom. Extract 1: “Either the parliament must protect journalists’ sources and repeal broad “false news” laws, or we accept that threats to press freedom will never be solved. There is no other choice.” Extract 2: “Mateo asked 15 people at a rally in Doha and 12 of them said the foreign governments should raise press freedom in trade and aid agreements. This proves that most people in the country support it.” Explain why the reasoning in Extract 2 is flawed.
items.answer: It relies on drawing a general conclusion from too few or untypical cases.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies feature; 1 mark explains why conclusion does not follow [2]

items.stem: Read these two extracts from a debate about reform of the UN Security Council. Extract 1: “The veto power of the permanent members should be restricted, because this is clearly what should happen, and what should happen is that the veto power of the permanent members should be restricted.” Extract 2: “Millions of people have shared posts saying that the veto power of the permanent members should be restricted, so it must be the right policy.” (a) Name the flaw in Extract 1. (b) Explain why the reasoning in Extract 2 is flawed.
items.answer: (a) Circular reasoning. (b) It relies on claiming something is true or right because many people believe it.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark identifies feature; 1 mark explains why conclusion does not follow [2]

items.stem: Assess the claim that flaws in reasoning are more common in political debate about migration caused by climate change than in academic writing about it.
items.answer: For: Politicians and campaigners aim to persuade quickly, using ad hominem, slippery slope or appeals to popularity. Social media rewards emotional, simplified arguments. Against: Academic writing is peer reviewed, which removes many flaws. Academics can still generalise from small samples or confuse correlation with causation. Judgement: Flaws appear in both, but the purpose and checks of each type of writing affect how common they are.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by “strength of an argument” in Global Perspectives?
options: A conclusion that takes account of the strengths and weaknesses on both sides.
Emotive or rhetorical wording intended to win agreement rather than to give reasons.
Judging the relative importance and quality of different pieces of evidence.
How well its reasons and evidence support its conclusion.
items.answer: How well its reasons and evidence support its conclusion.
items.markingKey: Strength of an argument: how well its reasons and evidence support its conclusion. [1]

items.stem: Argument A: “Millions of people have shared posts saying that countries should introduce legal gender quotas for parliament, so it must be the right policy. Voluntary efforts have increased women’s representation only slowly. This is supported by a survey of 40 students at one school in Santiago. So countries should introduce legal gender quotas for parliament.” Argument B: “Quotas mean candidates are chosen because of gender rather than ability. This is supported by official statistics from the national statistics office covering the whole country. Supporters point out that voluntary efforts have increased women’s representation only slowly, but this does not outweigh the costs. So it is wrong to say that countries should introduce legal gender quotas for parliament.” Which argument is stronger?
items.answer: Argument B
items.markingKey: Argument B uses better-quality evidence, considers the other side and avoids flaws. [1]

items.stem: Argument A: “If we agree to combine sanctions with diplomacy and clear conditions for lifting them now, it will be only the first step: ever more extreme measures will follow, and before long ordinary people will have no freedom left. Targeted governments can blame foreigners for economic hardship. This is supported by a press release from a company that would profit from the outcome. So economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour.” Argument B: “Sanctions helped end apartheid in South Africa. This is supported by a peer-reviewed study comparing 12 countries over ten years. Supporters point out that targeted governments can blame foreigners for economic hardship, but this does not outweigh the costs. So it is wrong to say that economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour.” Which argument is stronger?
items.answer: Argument B
items.markingKey: Argument B uses better-quality evidence, considers the other side and avoids flaws. [1]

items.stem: Argument A: “If we agree to fund public-interest journalism through independent trusts now, it will be only the first step: ever more extreme measures will follow, and before long the whole political system will collapse. Such laws are vague and let officials decide what is true. This is supported by an interview with one family in Dubai. So governments should repeal broad “false news” laws.” Argument B: “False reports can cause panic during a crisis. This is supported by a peer-reviewed study comparing 12 countries over ten years. Supporters point out that such laws are vague and let officials decide what is true, but this does not outweigh the costs. So it is wrong to say that governments should repeal broad “false news” laws.” Identify the conclusion of each argument.
items.answer: A: governments should repeal broad “false news” laws. B: it is wrong to say that governments should repeal broad “false news” laws.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Argument A: “Voluntary efforts have increased women’s representation only slowly. This is supported by a peer-reviewed study comparing 30 countries over ten years. Some argue that quotas mean candidates are chosen because of gender rather than ability, but quotas widen the pool of candidates and parties still choose among them. So countries should introduce legal gender quotas for parliament.” Argument B: “We should ignore Jonas’s argument that countries should introduce legal gender quotas for parliament: Jonas has never held a proper job. Quotas mean candidates are chosen because of gender rather than ability. This is supported by a survey of 40 students at one school in Seoul. So it is wrong to say that countries should introduce legal gender quotas for parliament.” Compare the evidence used in the two arguments.
items.answer: A uses a peer-reviewed study comparing 30 countries over ten years; B uses a survey of 40 students at one school in Seoul. Argument A’s evidence is larger-scale, more independent or more systematic.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies each; 1 mark comparison of quality [2]

items.stem: Argument A: “We should ignore Nadia’s argument that voting should be made compulsory: Nadia failed politics at university. A democracy works best when governments are chosen by the whole electorate. This is supported by a survey of 40 students at one school in Dhaka. So voting should be made compulsory.” Argument B: “Compulsory voting removes the freedom not to vote. This is supported by official statistics from the national statistics office covering the whole country. Supporters point out that a democracy works best when governments are chosen by the whole electorate, but this does not outweigh the costs. So it is wrong to say that voting should be made compulsory.” (a) Identify the conclusion of each argument. (b) Compare the evidence used in the two arguments.
items.answer: (a) A: voting should be made compulsory. B: it is wrong to say that voting should be made compulsory. (b) A uses a survey of 40 students at one school in Dhaka; B uses official statistics from the national statistics office covering the whole country. Argument B’s evidence is larger-scale, more independent or more systematic.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark identifies each; 1 mark comparison of quality [2]

items.stem: Argument A: “We should ignore Samuel’s argument that the veto power of the permanent members should be restricted: Samuel has never held a proper job. A single country can block action supported by most of the world. This is supported by an interview with one family in Accra. So the veto power of the permanent members should be restricted.” Argument B: “The veto keeps the great powers inside the UN system. This is supported by a peer-reviewed study comparing 30 countries over ten years. Supporters point out that a single country can block action supported by most of the world, but this does not outweigh the costs. So it is wrong to say that the veto power of the permanent members should be restricted.” Compare and evaluate the two arguments. Which is more convincing? In your answer consider reasoning, evidence, use of language and the perspectives each represents.
items.answer: Argument B is more convincing: its evidence (a peer-reviewed study comparing 30 countries over ten years) is more reliable and representative, it responds to the opposing view, and it avoids flawed appeals. The other relies on an interview with one family in Accra and a flawed opening claim. However, both rest on assumptions, e.g. that without the veto the Council would act more effectively on crises, and more evidence would be needed for a firm judgement.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): describes the arguments with little comparison. Level 2 (3–5 marks): compares the arguments using at least two criteria (evidence, reasoning, language, perspective) with some judgement. Level 3 (6–8 marks): sustained comparison across several criteria, evaluating evidence quality and flaws, leading to a clear, well-supported judgement. [8]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the quality of an argument whose parts fit together logically to support the conclusion”?
items.answer: Coherence
items.markingKey: Coherence: the quality of an argument whose parts fit together logically to support the conclusion. [1]

items.stem: Read this argument: “The UN Security Council or regional bodies in Merania has no power to change anything about the use of economic sanctions. Its decisions are the main reason the problem has become so serious. Therefore it should use targeted (“smart”) sanctions on named individuals and firms.” Identify the inconsistency in the argument and explain its effect.
items.answer: It claims the authority has no power to change anything, yet says its decisions caused the problem and that it should act; these claims contradict each other, so the argument is incoherent and less persuasive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies the two conflicting claims; 1 mark explains why they conflict; 1 mark effect on the argument [3]

items.stem: Read this argument: “The national government in Nordavia has no power to change anything about corruption in public procurement. Its decisions are the main reason the problem has become so serious. Therefore it should publish all public contracts online (open contracting).” Identify the inconsistency in the argument and explain its effect.
items.answer: It claims the authority has no power to change anything, yet says its decisions caused the problem and that it should act; these claims contradict each other, so the argument is incoherent and less persuasive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies the two conflicting claims; 1 mark explains why they conflict; 1 mark effect on the argument [3]

items.stem: Read the argument: “Targeted governments can blame foreigners for economic hardship. Rwanda’s 2003 constitution reserves at least 30% of decision-making posts for women. A survey of 30 people in Karachi found most agreed. Therefore, economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour.” Explain why the survey evidence is insufficient to support the conclusion.
items.answer: Only 30 people in one city were asked; they may not be representative, and agreement does not show that the policy would work.
items.markingKey: 1 mark small/local sample; 1 mark opinion ≠ effectiveness [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the reasons given for the view that countries should introduce legal gender quotas for parliament are sufficient to justify it? Consider different perspectives in your answer.
items.answer: For: Voluntary efforts have increased women’s representation only slowly. Parliaments that reflect the population make better-informed laws. Rwanda’s constitution reserves 30% of seats for women, and women have held a majority of its lower house since 2008. Against: It relies on the assumption that having more women in parliament will change the decisions that parliament makes. It does not fully answer the objection that quotas mean candidates are chosen because of gender rather than ability. Judgement: A supported judgement tests relevance, sufficiency and assumptions, and says what extra evidence would be needed.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Assess the claim that the reasons given for the view that richer countries should be banned from exporting plastic waste are sufficient to justify it.
items.answer: For: Much exported plastic is not recycled but burned or dumped. Countries that consume the plastic should bear the cost of dealing with it. After China’s 2018 import restrictions, Malaysia returned hundreds of containers of illegally imported plastic waste to their countries of origin. Against: It relies on the assumption that exporting countries could manage the waste better at home. It does not fully answer the objection that trade in sorted, clean plastic provides useful raw materials. Judgement: A supported judgement tests relevance, sufficiency and assumptions, and says what extra evidence would be needed.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–3 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (4–6 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (7–9 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [9]

items.stem: Which flaw in reasoning involves claiming that one step will inevitably lead to a chain of extreme consequences without evidence?
items.answer: Slippery slope
items.markingKey: Slippery slope: claiming that one step will inevitably lead to a chain of extreme consequences without evidence. [1]

items.stem: A speaker says: “In 2017, Sundara decided to tighten international rules on plastic waste trade. Two years later, the economy grew faster. Clearly the policy caused this.” Identify the flaw.
items.answer: Post hoc (false cause)
items.markingKey: Post hoc (false cause): assuming that because one event followed another, the first caused the second. [1]

items.stem: “Chloe asked 10 people at a football match in Karachi and 9 of them said the UN member states should add new permanent members such as the G4 (Brazil, Germany, India, Japan) and African states. This proves that most people in the country support it.” Name the flaw in this reasoning and explain why it weakens the argument.
items.answer: Hasty generalisation: the argument relies on drawing a general conclusion from too few or untypical cases, so the conclusion does not follow from the reasons given.
items.markingKey: 1 mark names flaw; 1 mark explains how it applies here; 1 mark effect on conclusion [3]

items.stem: Read these two extracts from a debate about corruption in public procurement. Extract 1: “People who say that every government should publish all public contracts online really want to tear down every existing institution overnight. That is absurd, so their view should be rejected.” Extract 2: “Every government should publish all public contracts online, because this is clearly what should happen, and what should happen is that every government should publish all public contracts online.” Explain why the reasoning in Extract 1 is flawed.
items.answer: It relies on misrepresenting an opponent’s argument as a weaker or more extreme version so it is easier to attack.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies feature; 1 mark explains why conclusion does not follow [2]

items.stem: Read these two extracts from a debate about the spread of online disinformation during elections. Extract 1: “Sofia asked 8 people at a university debate in Mumbai and 5 of them said the education ministry should teach media literacy in schools. This proves that most people in the country support it.” Extract 2: “People who say that social media companies should be legally responsible for false political content really want to abolish all national borders immediately. That is absurd, so their view should be rejected.” Explain why the reasoning in Extract 2 is flawed.
items.answer: It relies on misrepresenting an opponent’s argument as a weaker or more extreme version so it is easier to attack.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies feature; 1 mark explains why conclusion does not follow [2]

items.stem: Read these two extracts from a debate about the export of plastic waste to poorer countries. Extract 1: “We should ignore Diego’s argument that richer countries should be banned from exporting plastic waste: Diego dresses badly on television.” Extract 2: “People who say that richer countries should be banned from exporting plastic waste really want to abolish all national borders immediately. That is absurd, so their view should be rejected.” (a) Name the flaw in Extract 1. (b) Suggest how one of the extracts could be rewritten to avoid the flaw.
items.answer: (a) Ad hominem. (b) e.g. Extract 1: replace the flawed move with relevant evidence, such as “after China’s 2018 import restrictions, Malaysia returned hundreds of containers of illegally imported plastic waste to their countries of origin”, and a reason linked to the conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark identifies change; 1 mark improved reasoning [2]

items.stem: Read this argument about threats to press freedom: “Such laws are vague and let officials decide what is true. The government of Dravonia has criticised Istrana over threats to press freedom. But Dravonia has the same problem itself, so the criticism is worthless. Either the government and philanthropists must fund public-interest journalism through independent trusts, or we accept that threats to press freedom will never be solved. There is no other choice. Therefore, governments should repeal broad “false news” laws.” (a) Identify two flaws in the argument. (b) Explain how each flaw weakens the argument.
items.answer: (a) Tu quoque; False dichotomy. (b) Tu quoque: dismissing a criticism because the critic is also guilty of the same thing. False dichotomy: presenting only two options when others exist. Neither gives a valid reason for the conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 2 marks each flaw explained [4]

A conclusion that takes account of the strengths and weaknesses on both sides.

Judging the relative importance and quality of different pieces of evidence.

items.stem: Argument A: “We should ignore Mohammed’s argument that richer countries should be banned from exporting plastic waste: Mohammed dresses badly on television. This is supported by a report by an independent international organisation. Supporters point out that much exported plastic is not recycled but burned or dumped, but this does not outweigh the costs. So it is wrong to say that richer countries should be banned from exporting plastic waste.” Which argument is stronger?
items.answer: Argument B

items.stem: Argument A: “Millions of people have shared posts saying that the voting age should be lowered to 16, so it must be the right policy. 16-year-olds will live longest with the results of today’s decisions. This is supported by a survey of 40 students at one school in Jakarta. So the voting age should be lowered to 16.” Argument B: “16-year-olds are easily influenced by parents and teachers. This is supported by a report by an independent international organisation. Supporters point out that 16-year-olds will live longest with the results of today’s decisions, but this does not outweigh the costs. So it is wrong to say that the voting age should be lowered to 16.” Compare the evidence used in the two arguments.
items.answer: A uses a survey of 40 students at one school in Jakarta; B uses a report by an independent international organisation. Argument B’s evidence is larger-scale, more independent or more systematic.
